extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary students, language learners, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and reflective guidance on poetic effect, language acquisition, choice of literary models, diction, metrical study, and editorial principles for literary/journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language acquisition by immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the language in the country itself by learning words with the objects before you and without the intermediation of the English terms; make it a regular part of study to call every, the minutest, thing by its [native] name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical routine: accompany a native (e.g., the pastor) around house, garden, farmyard, &c., and name everything in the target tongue; use advertisements, farces, jest books, and children's conversation to gain a home-like acquaintance beyond polite literature. (Passage: 'it may be useful... the incalculable advantage which I derived from learning all the words, that could possibly be so learned, with the objects before me, and without the intermediation of the English terms.' )

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from everyday speakers and observe speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire idiomatic speech by consulting ordinary native speakers — mothers, children, the common man in the market — and by watching the movement of their mouths while they speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Luther's counsel: 'one must ask the mother in the house, the children in the lanes, ... the common man in the market, ... and look at the mover of their mouths while they are talking, and thereafter interpret.' This emphasizes low-register, living usage over bookish forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely among master poets and historical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Study a wide range of canonical poets and historical poetic traditions (Minnesinger, metrical romances, Hans Sachs, Pindar, Chaucer, Dante, Milton, etc.) to form taste and judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through representative specimens and successors; repeated perusal of such authors trains the reader to discern genuine style. ('From the works of Opitz... my feelings justified the verdict, and I seemed to have acquired from them a sort of tact for what is genuine in the style of later writers.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combination of natural imagery and mysterious/sublime belief
rubrics_metrics.description: To deepen emotional and religious effect in poetry, combine purely natural images with a belief in something mysterious that elevates the feelings above their natural pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'Most interesting is it to consider the effect, when the feelings are wrought above the natural pitch by the belief of something mysterious, while all the images are purely natural. Then it is, that religion and poetry strike deepest.' Use this interplay to intensify resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect poetic content with moral and political feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and cultivate the close connexion between poetic genius and the love of liberty and genuine reformation; moral engagement often deepens poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Pindar, Chaucer, Dante, Milton (and even Hans Sachs) as examples where poetic genius links to love of liberty and reformation, suggesting theme choice and moral purpose contribute to a poem's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer pure diction; avoid pedantic barbarisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hybridized, pedantic diction (e.g., excessive Latinisms grafted into the vernacular) that corrupts clarity and sweetness of style; seek models of pure diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical caution: 'Within less than a century after Luther's death the German was inundated with pedantic barbarisms... Almost every third word is a Latin word with a Germanized ending.' Use established models (Opitz, Silessian poets) who restored the language and remain 'models of pure diction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Study metrical paraphrases and older forms to learn rhythm and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Read metrical paraphrases and older vernacular poetic forms (e.g., Ottfried's metrical paraphrase, Theotiscun, Minnesinger) to master flow, rhythm, and metrical devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points to specific pleasure and instruction in such works: 'There is a flow, and a tender enthusiasm in the following lines... which, even in the translation, ... will not, I flatter myself, fail to interest the reader.' Use these texts to internalize metre and cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial principle: fixed announced principles and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: In conducting a journal or public literary platform, establish fixed and announced principles and refuse to deviate in favour of any party or event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition for accepting editorship: 'the paper should thenceforward be conducted on certain fixed and announced principles, and that I should neither be obliged nor requested to deviate from them in favor of any party or any event.' The author argues a moderate, principled stance often yields greater long-term influence.
